newHazards.summary: H1 creates the exact configuration round 3's M3 rule was written for, without the disclosure: the Orders tab label and Profile StatCard now read the uncapped meta.total (e.g. "Orders (120)") while the Order History table at :3237 renders `filteredOrders` — at most the endpoint's take:50 page — with no truncation note anywhere on the tab. Before H1 the label matched the rows; now a 120-order customer is told 120 and shown 50. The status Select at :3221 also filters only those 50, so "Completed" on such a customer silently shows a subset. Designed consequence of the lead's ruling ("the list stays a display budget"), so not a blocker — but a one-line note gated on `orderCount > allOrders.length` would close it, and it is the same class the batch just fixed on the statement surfaces.

The H5 note over-fires. `ledgerTruncated` is the WHOLE-statement flag — getMyStatement sets `transactionsTruncated = invoicesTruncated || creditNotesTruncated` — so a buyer with 51+ invoices and only 2 credit notes gets `activeCreditsTruncated === true` and reads "Showing 2 of the latest active credits", implying hidden credits that do not exist. This is literally the predicate the ruling specified, so it is designed, not a defect; closing it would need a per-entity truncation flag on the statement DTO (creditNotesTruncated), which is an API change out of round-4 scope.

H2's stated goal ("every returned money figure rounded") is complete only for the six header figures the ruling named. The transactions ledger rows both methods return still carry raw floats: `runningBalance: -(Number(i.total) - i.amountPaid)` at :417 (getMyStatement) and :1132 (getStatementForOperator), where `amountPaid` is `sumConfirmed`, an unrounded reduce (apps/api/src/invoices/payment-predicates.ts:44-46). Two 0.1/0.2 confirmed payments on a $100 invoice return runningBalance -99.69999999999999 over the wire. Mitigated in practice: web/mobile render these through fmt() and the buyer credit filter uses a dust-tolerant `> 0.001` threshold — so this is contract dust, not a visible wrong number. Worth one `roundMoney` on the two row builders in a later round.

Empty-card path: the Active Credits card is gated on `hasActiveCredit` (the uncapped availableCredit, from round 3's M3) while its rows come from the capped ledger. A buyer whose 50 most recent credit notes are all fully used but who holds an older active credit gets availableCredit > 0 with `creditRows` empty — the card renders its header, the note "Showing 0 of the latest active credits; the wallet total includes everything", and an empty divider block. Truthful and disclosed, but the zero-row card reads oddly; suppressing the rows block (or the card) when `activeCredits.length === 0` would tidy it.

`meta` is optional on CustomerOrdersResponse, so `orderCount = ordersResult?.meta?.total ?? 0`. If a response ever arrived without meta, the tab would drop its count and the Profile StatCard would read "0" while the table below renders up to 50 rows — a self-contradicting screen rather than a loud failure. Unreachable against the current endpoint (findOrders always returns meta), and the optionality is deliberate per the doc comment; noted only so a future response-shape change is known to fail silently here.

review.reasoning:
All five leftovers are genuinely closed, and I verified the load-bearing claims myself rather than trusting the executor report: I re-ran the two touched API spec files (`npx jest src/customers/customers.service.spec.ts src/invoices/invoices.service.spec.ts --maxWorkers=2` → 2 suites / 405 tests passed), the web typecheck (`npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json` → clean, exit 0), and `prettier --check` on all 7 touched files (\"All matched files use Prettier code style!\"). I also refuted each claim at the source: meta.total is a genuinely uncapped `order.count` with the same where as the take:50 findMany (customers.service.ts:817-825), so H1's count is honest and the hook's new generic has exactly one caller; all four figures the H2 ruling named are roundMoney-wrapped in the method that owns them, in BOTH statement methods, with one pin per method whose fixture proves its own dust via `expect(0.1 + 0.2).not.toBe(0.3)`; the H3 pin's expected orderBy matches the impl's actual `Object.hasOwn` fallback line for line; the orphaned note is gone from the payments page (grep returns zero hits, import included) while the one legitimate use above the operator ledger survives; and the H5 note is keyed on the exact `ledgerTruncated || creditRows.length > activeCredits.length` predicate with nothing derived from the six rows. The two H5 deviations from the ruling's literal text (a computed numerator instead of \"6\", an inline

instead of the fixed-prose component) are both strictly more truthful and reversible in one line — I judge them accepted deviations, not designMismatch, and flag them for the lead rather than spending a round on them. No regression appeared in the round-3 work these edits sit on. The five new hazards are all low or minor and none is a wrong money value: the strongest, the Orders tab now showing an honest 120 above a silent 50-row table, is a direct and knowing consequence of the lead's own H1 ruling (\"the list stays a display budget\") and closes with a one-line note, so it belongs in the close-out or a follow-up, not in another executor round. Land.
